dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: BASTION SPIRE — RELIC COURT

dialogueInline.speaker: DOMINION
dialogueInline.text: We can stabilize the Gate with a permanent Fleet schedule and verified patrol assignment.

dialogueInline.speaker: HALEV
dialogueInline.text: You can stabilize the passage. If the schedule requires Auric's permission to be revised every time someone on your side changes a command, that isn't the same as control over our traffic.

dialogueInline.speaker: DOMINION
dialogueInline.text: I didn't say you would lose control of your ports.

dialogueInline.speaker: HALEV
dialogueInline.text: You didn't say we would keep it either. That's why we're still talking.

dialogueInline.speaker: JEX
dialogueInline.text: I can connect the purchases. I can show the people paid to make the market angry, and the relays bought before the Shatterforge lock. I can't make an account number confess to being one particular person.

dialogueInline.speaker: DOMINION
dialogueInline.text: The ledgers are authenticated?

dialogueInline.speaker: JEX
dialogueInline.text: By more than me. Which was the point of releasing them. A very expensive point, I might add.

dialogueInline.speaker: ABBY
dialogueInline.text: You're calling it an emergency exception. How many times does something have to work before we stop calling it an exception?

dialogueInline.speaker: DOMINION
dialogueInline.text: It worked under exceptional conditions. Those captains aren't in the Fleet chain.

dialogueInline.speaker: ABBY
dialogueInline.text: Exactly. And they kept the lane open anyway. You don't have to command them to rely on what they agreed to do.

dialogueInline.speaker: DOMINION
dialogueInline.text: And when one of your captains changes their mind during a battle?

dialogueInline.speaker: DOMINION
dialogueInline.text: I have a report on an escort officer who left formation to recover a civilian tug. Another ship had to expose itself to cover the gap. The tug was recovered. We were fortunate there was no second attack. If you had asked the families on the tug, they would have wanted that officer to turn. If you'd asked the civilians behind the screen, they might have wanted the ship to stay.

dialogueInline.speaker: HALEV
dialogueInline.text: We don't know what the families behind the screen would have said.

dialogueInline.speaker: DOMINION
dialogueInline.text: That's precisely my concern. The people making these decisions can't canvass the people they're going to endanger. They need a structure they trust when the time to think has run out.

dialogueInline.speaker: ABBY
dialogueInline.text: I trust the captains who stood with me. That doesn't mean I know what every one of them will do tomorrow.

dialogueInline.speaker: DOMINION
dialogueInline.text: Then on what basis can I put Fleet ships beside them?

dialogueInline.speaker: ABBY
dialogueInline.text: You ask what each captain can promise, and you put the promise where the next captain can inspect it. No one gets to discover in the middle of a crossing that a Shard captain agreed to defend a different lane from the one you were counting on. And if a captain refuses, we don't write them into the formation anyway.

dialogueInline.speaker: DOMINION
dialogueInline.text: That's a schedule, not a chain of command.

dialogueInline.speaker: ABBY
dialogueInline.text: Yes. That's why it might work between us.

dialogueInline.speaker: ABBY
dialogueInline.text: Then the other people on the line deserve to know it. That's why we need a procedure we can inspect, not a promise about how good everyone is.

dialogueInline.speaker: HALEV
dialogueInline.text: In the last three months, I have signed emergency orders to house people in places they didn't own, ration food people had already bought and ask captains to protect convoys they weren't obligated to escort. Every signature was supposed to solve an immediate problem. Each one left somebody owing somebody else something they hadn't agreed to.

dialogueInline.speaker: DOMINION
dialogueInline.text: Government cannot operate without emergency authority.

dialogueInline.speaker: HALEV
dialogueInline.text: I know. I used it. I'm asking what keeps the emergency from becoming the ordinary way we govern. These people will still have to buy fuel and heat their homes thirty days from now.

dialogueInline.speaker: JEX
dialogueInline.text: Some of them will still be trying to collect payment from me. Since we're naming the injured parties, I'd appreciate a little precision.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: RELIC COURT — ACCORD NEGOTIATION

dialogueInline.speaker: BILLIE
dialogueInline.text: You've built a beautiful agreement. I particularly like the part where Fleet gets to decide when the emergency is serious enough to own everything.

dialogueInline.speaker: VENN
dialogueInline.text: That language was intended for immediate rescue coordination.

dialogueInline.speaker: BILLIE
dialogueInline.text: Then why does it say command? And whose rescue are we coordinating when the person giving the order can also declare what counts as danger?

dialogueInline.speaker: DOMINION
dialogueInline.text: You are not a party to these negotiations.

dialogueInline.speaker: BILLIE
dialogueInline.text: I noticed. My ship has spent months being told where it may travel by people who never asked me to sit at their table. I've come to offer the table a familiar experience.

dialogueInline.speaker: ABBY
dialogueInline.text: Billie, what do you want it to say?

panelPlan: The draft Accord leaves a broad clause allowing Fleet to assume unified control during a corridor emergency. Billie Rusk arrives uninvited and finds the clause.
Abby watches her oldest friend challenge the clause without claiming the moral high ground.
directionInline: Use supplied Rex Fleet references; retain scene continuity; exact scripted lettering only.
sourceActionBeats: *The draft Accord leaves a broad clause allowing Fleet to assume unified control during a corridor emergency. Billie Rusk arrives uninvited and finds the clause before anyone can usher her away.*
*Abby watches her oldest friend challenge the clause without claiming the moral high ground.*

dialogueInline.speaker: BILLIE
dialogueInline.text: That a ship's captain can protect civilians without becoming somebody else's property for thirty days. That the route doesn't disappear because one faction is angry. That if Fleet wants a Shard ship to move, Fleet asks, and the captain has to answer for whatever they decide.

dialogueInline.speaker: DOMINION
dialogueInline.text: A chain of command cannot operate on requests.

dialogueInline.speaker: BILLIE
dialogueInline.text: Then don't call three different chains one chain. They aren't. They didn't become one because we had a frightening evening.

dialogueInline.speaker: HALEV
dialogueInline.text: If one captain sees a civilian collision risk and has to wait for three authorities to agree, we're going to kill somebody with perfect courtesy.

panelPlan: Halev looks at the clause. He has spent months resisting a Fleet permanent presence, yet the evacuation proved he needs ships he does not control.
directionInline: Use supplied Rex Fleet references; retain scene continuity; exact scripted lettering only.
sourceActionBeats: *Halev looks at the clause. He has spent months resisting a Fleet permanent presence, yet the evacuation proved he needs ships he does not control.*

dialogueInline.speaker: BILLIE
dialogueInline.text: Then don't make them wait. Give a captain the power to protect people in immediate danger. Make them tell everyone else what they did and why. Don't give the captain the power to claim every other ship afterward.

dialogueInline.speaker: DOMINION
dialogueInline.text: Emergency authority without a clear limit can be abused.

dialogueInline.speaker: BILLIE
dialogueInline.text: Yes. You may have noticed I have some experience with that.

dialogueInline.speaker: VENN
dialogueInline.text: What you're proposing puts a heavy responsibility on whoever recognizes the danger first.

dialogueInline.speaker: BILLIE
dialogueInline.text: It already does. You can pretend the rule will keep them safe from making a terrible choice, or you can make certain the choice is recorded and answerable afterward.

dialogueInline.speaker: SELENE
dialogueInline.text: That would require preserving decisions made by other factions even when the original authority disputed them.

panelPlan: No one can tell whether she means her own orders or those she obeyed. Tess, who knows both histories, doesn't rescue her from the silence.
directionInline: Use supplied Rex Fleet references; retain scene continuity; exact scripted lettering only.
sourceActionBeats: *No one can tell whether she means her own orders or those she obeyed. Tess, who knows both histories, doesn't rescue her from the silence.*

dialogueInline.speaker: HALEV
dialogueInline.text: It would also require my council to admit that a Verge pilot can be wrong, and that Fleet might save us without being entitled to run us.

dialogueInline.speaker: JEX
dialogueInline.text: A clause requiring everyone to admit they may be wrong. I expect it to be the shortest agreement in human history.

dialogueInline.speaker: TESS
dialogueInline.text: You could stay for the signing.

dialogueInline.speaker: BILLIE
dialogueInline.text: I've done enough damage to contracts this year.

dialogueInline.speaker: TESS
dialogueInline.text: You could stay long enough to hear what you've changed.

dialogueInline.speaker: BILLIE
dialogueInline.text: I'd rather hear about it from the pilots after they've flown under it. A signed piece of paper can be very agreeable to everyone who never has to maneuver a ship.

dialogueInline.speaker: ABBY
dialogueInline.text: Are you going to obstruct the trial?

She looks at the coin on the amended page. The room expects a signature, a handshake or a new allegiance. She gives them none of those things.
Billie turns toward her. They have said far worse things to each other during this season; both seem to remember them.

dialogueInline.text: No. But I'm not going to swear loyalty to an agreement I helped argue with. My crew hasn't consented to it. If they want to join an escort, they can tell me, and I'll decide whether Ashfang can safely cover them.

dialogueInline.speaker: ABBY
dialogueInline.text: That's all I was asking.

dialogueInline.speaker: BILLIE
dialogueInline.text: It wasn't. You were asking whether I can be trusted to stay out of the way. I don't know if you can trust me. I know I wouldn't have trusted myself six months ago.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: RELIC COURT — ACCORD TERMS

dialogueInline.speaker: SELENE
dialogueInline.text: Shared measured windows. Separate ship command. Mixed escorts by independent consent. No unilateral transfer of civilian witnesses. No permanent assumption of port authority. Thirty days, then review.

dialogueInline.speaker: DOMINION
dialogueInline.text: And a provision allowing any party to withdraw if the measurements cease to support safe transit.

dialogueInline.speaker: JIA
dialogueInline.text: That's essential. A political signature cannot make an unstable field stable.

dialogueInline.speaker: HALEV
dialogueInline.text: Nor can a safe field force a captain to be cooperative.

dialogueInline.speaker: VENN
dialogueInline.text: I don't know whether our governments can live with this.

dialogueInline.speaker: ABBY
dialogueInline.text: Neither do I. We can find out without asking the civilians to wait for us to like each other.

panelPlan: Selene reads back the operational terms; the officials hear their own compromises in the plain language of someone who will archive them.
Venn and Abby sign the bounded working terms, not a universal peace.
They turn toward practical preparations rather than declaring a new era.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: AURIC GATE — DUSK

dialogueInline.speaker: SECOND
dialogueInline.text: Verge timing agrees. Fleet return is within tolerance. Shard return arrived a fraction late.

dialogueInline.speaker: NAOMI
dialogueInline.text: Late enough to matter?

dialogueInline.speaker: SECOND
dialogueInline.text: Not yet. It is the first time three people have agreed on an error rather than which one of them caused it.

dialogueInline.speaker: VENN
dialogueInline.text: All three confirmations received. Deka, the lane is yours to cover.

dialogueInline.speaker: DEKA
dialogueInline.text: Understood. I'd like our shield to survive this agreement. Engineering, don't let anyone borrow its power for a demonstration.

dialogueInline.speaker: NAOMI
dialogueInline.text: Don't be too friendly. Give them proper spacing or you'll both spend the next hour explaining how we managed to collide during a peace trial.

dialogueInline.speaker: PILOT
dialogueInline.text: I thought it was Fleet drift.

dialogueInline.speaker: TESS
dialogueInline.text: Of course you did. It's a very economical explanation. Unfortunately the clock is yours.

dialogueInline.text: SHARDFALL CITADEL

dialogueInline.speaker: TRADE MASK
dialogueInline.text: They are running a single certified route on borrowed cooperation. One delayed shipment will put the market back on its knees.

dialogueInline.speaker: FEAR MASK
dialogueInline.text: They have taught civilians to trust copied clocks. Copies can disagree. People can be shown the difference.

dialogueInline.speaker: RAID MASK
dialogueInline.text: Let them demonstrate the schedule until it becomes valuable. Then we'll know precisely what they cannot afford to lose.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: RELIC COURT — ANALYSIS DESK

dialogueInline.speaker: SELENE
dialogueInline.text: One record calls it disciplined Fleet restraint. Another calls it Verge navigation. The third says independent Shard captains kept the guns off the lane.

dialogueInline.speaker: JIA
dialogueInline.text: All three describe actions that happened.

dialogueInline.speaker: SELENE
dialogueInline.text: Yes. None is a complete account of why they happened.

dialogueInline.speaker: JIA
dialogueInline.text: Then record the measurements separately from the motives. We can verify the clocks. We can ask people what they intended. We can't calibrate an intention.

dialogueInline.speaker: SELENE
dialogueInline.text: When I was younger, I believed the work was to recover the right version of events. You find enough original records, you identify the corrections, and eventually the noise goes away.

dialogueInline.speaker: JIA
dialogueInline.text: Has it?

dialogueInline.speaker: SELENE
dialogueInline.text: No. It has accumulated more very well documented reasons to disagree.

dialogueInline.speaker: JIA
dialogueInline.text: That sounds like progress.

panelPlan: Relic Court analysis desk. Selene compares Fleet, Verge, and Shard records of the same crossing. The timestamps agree; the explanations don't.
Selene closes the first version of the archive and looks at a blank comparative record. It bothers her that the blank space is not a failure of scholarship but.
directionInline: Use supplied Rex Fleet references; retain scene continuity; exact scripted lettering only.
sourceActionBeats: *Relic Court analysis desk. Selene compares Fleet, Verge, and Shard records of the same crossing. The timestamps agree; the explanations don't.*

*Selene closes the first version of the archive and looks at a blank comparative record. It bothers her that the blank space is not a failure of scholarship but a truthful description of the evidence.*

dialogueInline.speaker: SELENE
dialogueInline.text: It's an irritating kind of progress. People expect history to tell them what happened. They don't want to be told three people acted for different reasons and that those reasons are part of what happened.

dialogueInline.speaker: JIA
dialogueInline.text: I can't explain the corridor's echoes. But now I can tell another scientist which measurements to repeat if they want to disagree with me. If the next result proves I was wrong, we still have learned something. Does your record allow that?

dialogueInline.speaker: SELENE
dialogueInline.text: It will have to. Otherwise the next government will decide which motive was proper and erase the others before anyone has time to object.

dialogueInline.speaker: JIA
dialogueInline.text: I like your profession better when it sounds like a laboratory.

dialogueInline.speaker: SELENE
dialogueInline.text: And I like yours better when it remembers who was aboard the ships.

They return to the records. Neither has won the conversation, and both have made the other person's work slightly harder and more useful.
Selene begins a new comparative record, uncomfortable but accurate. The historical explanation remains unsettled.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: AURIC — GOVERNOR HALL

dialogueInline.speaker: NAOMI
dialogueInline.text: I hear you're charging for people to make sense of free route data now.

dialogueInline.speaker: JEX
dialogueInline.text: Expertise remains stubbornly billable.

dialogueInline.speaker: NAOMI
dialogueInline.text: And the private refuge routes?

dialogueInline.speaker: JEX
dialogueInline.text: Still private when their disclosure would hurt the people using them. Transparency is not the same thing as leaving every door unlocked.

dialogueInline.speaker: NAOMI
dialogueInline.text: You haven't heard from Tali.

dialogueInline.speaker: JEX
dialogueInline.text: No. I keep expecting to. I don't know whether that means I'm hopeful or incapable of learning.

dialogueInline.speaker: NAOMI
dialogueInline.text: You can be both.

dialogueInline.speaker: JEX
dialogueInline.text: I used to be the person who could find somebody. You gave me a name and a debt and I'd tell you which berth to knock on. I was very good at it.

dialogueInline.speaker: NAOMI
dialogueInline.text: You still are.

panelPlan: Auric governor hall. Naomi finds Jex looking at his old private route token. He has rebuilt part of his trade business around publicly verifiable timing rather.
Jex turns the token over. Its worn edge has been polished by a habit of his thumb, not by any special material. Naomi has been careful not to ask to see what.

dialogueInline.speaker: JEX
dialogueInline.text: I haven't found my own sister.

dialogueInline.speaker: NAOMI
dialogueInline.text: Your routes can tell you where a ship went. They can't tell you what a person did after they stopped answering.

dialogueInline.speaker: JEX
dialogueInline.text: That's not much help.

dialogueInline.speaker: NAOMI
dialogueInline.text: I wasn't trying to help. I was trying not to lie to you.

dialogueInline.speaker: JEX
dialogueInline.text: Her last message was about moving families. Not about herself. I keep rereading it as if she left me an instruction I haven't understood.

dialogueInline.speaker: NAOMI
dialogueInline.text: She may have been busy doing exactly what she said she was doing.

dialogueInline.speaker: JEX
dialogueInline.text: Yes.

dialogueInline.text: GRAVEFIRE — CIVILIAN BERTH

dialogueInline.speaker: CHILD
dialogueInline.text: They said five minutes.

dialogueInline.speaker: TESS
dialogueInline.text: People who work in arrival offices are very optimistic about minutes.

dialogueInline.speaker: CHILD
dialogueInline.text: Do they always come back?

dialogueInline.speaker: TESS
dialogueInline.text: I can't promise you that about every person. I can tell you your parent is in that office, and the person at the desk knows you're waiting. Would it help if we sat where they can see us?

*The child nods. Tess shifts a crate to make space, using the uninjured arm. They wait together without a grand lesson about the Accord.*

dialogueInline.text: THUNDERBREAK — NEXT MORNING

dialogueInline.speaker: NAOMI
dialogueInline.text: You remember what I said before you left for the tribunal?

dialogueInline.speaker: VENN
dialogueInline.text: You told me to come back with something Auric could use.

dialogueInline.speaker: NAOMI
dialogueInline.text: Yes. I thought you might come back with a repair crew and a very long speech about it.

dialogueInline.speaker: VENN
dialogueInline.text: I've sent the crews. Would you prefer the speech now?

dialogueInline.speaker: NAOMI
dialogueInline.text: No. Please don't spoil it.

dialogueInline.speaker: VENN
dialogueInline.text: We sent people who can repair it. Not people who can redesign it into a Fleet coupling.

dialogueInline.speaker: NAOMI
dialogueInline.text: That's more reassuring than you know.

dialogueInline.speaker: VENN
dialogueInline.text: I suspect I know a little more than I did before the tribunal.

dialogueInline.speaker: NAOMI
dialogueInline.text: I can't promise I won't be furious with you the next time Fleet takes a useful thing away. Or that I won't blame you for some of it even when it's not your order.

dialogueInline.speaker: VENN
dialogueInline.text: I wouldn't ask you to promise that.

dialogueInline.speaker: NAOMI
dialogueInline.text: Good. I still don't like having to ask your officers whether I'm allowed to use equipment to fix my own station.

dialogueInline.speaker: VENN
dialogueInline.text: Then ask the people who own it. They should be told what the loan actually allows. I've learned that a favor with a hidden command in it isn't much of a favor.
